newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli mutual funds show signs of recovery.
newsitem.headline: Israeli mutual funds show signs of recovery.

text.p: Israeli mutual funds may be set for a recovery after a three-year slump during which they suffered net redemptions of 20 billion shekels, Meitav Investments and Securities said on Tuesday.
"There is a change in the trend....there are already symptoms of recovery," said Zvi Steptak, joint managing director of Meitav, which tracks developments in the mutual and provident funds.
"In January, we expect that there will be a net inflow of money into the stock funds, unless something happens towards the end of the month," he told Reuters.
Bond funds, he added, would probably register redemptions in January, but at much lower levels.

Israel's 302 mutual funds posted redemptions of 4.12 billion shekels last year, following withdrawals of 4.8 billion shekels in 1995 and 11.2 billion shekels in 1994. At the end of 1996, they had 13.55 billion shekels under management, a figure Meitav said was the lowest level in real terms since May 1989.
On a monthly basis, however, the trend has begun to change. Since they peaked at 571 million shekels in July 1996, monthly redemptions have been falling and were 177 million shekels in December.

"There were redemptions in December, but they were the lowest of the year," said Stepak. "The 177 million shekels was in all categories. When you look at stock funds in December they were even lower. Most of the redemptions were in fixed-income funds."
Caram funds, which invest in small capitalisation shares, even posted a net inflow, Meitav said.

The mutual fund industry's turnaround comes as the Israeli stock market marks the 10th week of a rally that has seen the Mishtanim index of top 100 shares rise about 26 percent. Mutual funds have begun posting positive returns.

The three-year wave of redemptions came as Israeli investors bailed out of the stock market and moved their money into bank deposits and other investments. Analysts say that the public's return will be a key element in the market's long-term recovery.
Mutual funds are one of the main vehicles small investors use to buy stocks.

Stepak said the investing public was not yet returning in big numbers. Much of the mutual fund buying now supporting stock prices is coming from portfolio managers and institutions buying mutual fund units and from fund managers' increasing their equities weighting, he said.
"The wave (of public buying) will widen after there is a correction....Stock prices have to ease back. They can't continue like this," Stepak said.
